stem: Which statement best describes black-box test techniques?
options: They derive tests from the internal structure of the test object, such as its branches
They can only be applied once the code has been written and compiled
They derive tests mainly from the tester's knowledge of failures in similar games
They derive tests from the specified behaviour of the test object, without reference to its internal structure
why: Black-box (specification-based) techniques analyse the specified behaviour of the test object and do not refer to how it is built inside.

distractorNotes.A: Adjacent-concept swap: tests from the internal structure are white-box tests.
distractorNotes.B: Black-box tests can be designed from the specification before any code exists; needing the implementation is a white-box trait.
distractorNotes.C: Tests built mainly on the tester's knowledge of past failures are experience-based.

stem: A studio rewrites the inventory system's C# code to make it faster. The required behaviour does not change. Which tests are most likely to stay useful without any changes?
options: Tests designed to reach 100% branch coverage of the old inventory code
Fault attacks aimed at the defects the old inventory code used to have
None: any change to the implementation makes all existing tests useless
Tests designed from the inventory requirements in the GDD
why: Black-box test cases depend only on the specified behaviour, so they stay useful when the implementation changes but the required behaviour does not.

distractorNotes.A: White-box tests depend on how the software is implemented; new code has new branches.
distractorNotes.B: An attack list tuned to the old code's typical defects may no longer fit the rewritten code; it is the least stable of the experience-based options here.
distractorNotes.C: Overgeneralisation: tests based on the unchanged specification are still valid.

stem: Which of the following is a characteristic of experience-based test techniques?
options: Their effectiveness depends heavily on the skills of the tester
They give an objective measure of how much of the code was exercised
They can only be used when a complete and detailed specification exists
They make black-box and white-box techniques unnecessary
why: Experience-based techniques use the tester's knowledge and experience, so how well they work depends heavily on the tester's skills.

distractorNotes.B: An objective measure of code coverage comes from white-box techniques.
distractorNotes.C: The reverse: experience-based techniques are useful when specifications are poor or missing.
distractorNotes.D: Overgeneralisation: they complement the other families and find defects the others miss; they do not replace them.

stem: You are a tester on a team where a developer shows you the control flow graph of a new pathfinding method and asks you to design tests until every decision outcome in it has been exercised. Which category of test technique are you using?
options: Black-box
Experience-based
Collaboration-based
White-box
why: The tests are based on the internal structure (the control flow graph and its decision outcomes): a white-box technique, branch testing.

distractorNotes.A: Black-box tests come from the specified behaviour, not from the control flow graph.
distractorNotes.B: Nothing here relies on the tester's experience; the structure of the code drives the tests.
distractorNotes.C: Collaboration-based approaches are about user stories, acceptance criteria and ATDD, not code structure.

stem: Match each test technique (1–4) with its category (a–c). 1. Decision table testing; 2. Branch testing; 3. Checklist-based testing; 4. Equivalence partitioning. a. Black-box; b. White-box; c. Experience-based.
why: Decision tables and EP are black-box techniques, branch testing is white-box, and checklist-based testing is experience-based.

distractorNotes.A: Checklist-based testing is experience-based, and EP is black-box: 3 and 4 are swapped.
distractorNotes.C: Decision table testing works from the specified rules: black-box, not experience-based.
distractorNotes.D: Branch testing uses the code structure (white-box) and EP uses the specification (black-box): 2 and 4 are swapped.

stem: Which statement about white-box test techniques is CORRECT?
options: Their test cases can be written from the GDD before any design or code exists
They are another name for experience-based techniques used by developers
They look only at what the player sees on screen, never at the code
Their test cases depend on how the software is designed, so they can only be created after the design or implementation exists
why: White-box test cases are derived from the internal structure, so they depend on the design and can only be created once it or the code exists.

distractorNotes.A: Writing tests from the GDD before any code exists describes black-box techniques.
distractorNotes.B: Category smear: white-box and experience-based are separate families, whoever uses them.
distractorNotes.C: Looking only at the visible behaviour is the black-box view; white-box looks at the structure.

stem: Test techniques support the tester in test analysis and test design. Which of the following do they NOT help the tester to do?
options: Set the priority of the defects reported during test execution
Define the test conditions
Identify the coverage items
Identify the test data
why: Test techniques help to define test conditions, identify coverage items and identify test data. Setting defect priority is part of defect management, not of test design.

distractorNotes.B: Defining test conditions is one of the things techniques help with (test analysis).
distractorNotes.C: Identifying coverage items, such as partitions or transitions, is a core use of techniques.
distractorNotes.D: Techniques help pick the test data, e.g. one value per partition.

stem: The lead of a playtest says: "There is no written spec for the new crafting UI, the build is due tomorrow, and our senior tester knows our games inside out." Which category of test technique fits this situation best?
options: White-box: tests designed from the branches of the crafting UI code
Black-box: decision tables built from the crafting specification
Experience-based: tests designed from the senior tester's knowledge and experience
Static analysis of the crafting UI scripts with a linter
why: With no specification, high time pressure and an experienced tester, experience-based techniques (e.g. exploratory testing) are the best fit.

distractorNotes.A: Possible in principle, but nothing in the situation points to working from the code, and it is slow under time pressure.
distractorNotes.B: Black-box techniques need a specification, and there is none.
distractorNotes.D: Static analysis is static testing, not one of the three families of test techniques.

stem: In the options menu, the mouse sensitivity field only lets the player type whole numbers. The game accepts 1 to 20 and rejects any other number. How many equivalence partitions should be identified?
why: Three partitions: 0 and below (invalid), 1–20 (valid), 21 and above (invalid). Values are rejected on both sides, so there is an invalid partition on each side.

distractorNotes.A: Off-by-one partition count: "valid" and "invalid" forgets that the invalid values lie on both sides of the range.
distractorNotes.C: 4 is the number of 2-value boundary values (0, 1, 20, 21), not the number of partitions.
distractorNotes.D: 6 is the 3-value BVA count for the valid partition's two boundaries; EP needs one test per partition.

stem: The GDD says: at sign-up the player enters their age (a whole number, 0 or more). Ages 13–17 get a teen account with chat limited to friends; ages 18 and over get a full account; ages under 13 are rejected with a message asking them to involve a parent. Which statement about the equivalence partitions is CORRECT?
options: There are two partitions: valid (13 and over) and invalid (under 13)
13–17 is an invalid partition, because chat is restricted for these players
There are two valid partitions (13–17 and 18 and over) and one invalid partition (0–12)
There are three valid partitions, because the spec also defines the message for ages under 13
why: The spec processes 13–17 and 18+ differently, so they are two valid partitions. Ages under 13 are rejected, so 0–12 is an invalid partition.

distractorNotes.A: Range-based thinking: 13 and over is processed in two different ways, so it is two partitions.
distractorNotes.B: Restricted is still processed as the spec defines: a valid partition. Valid does not mean "full access".
distractorNotes.D: Values the test object should reject are invalid, even when the spec describes the error message.

stem: A loot function takes a roll from 1 to 100: 1–60 gives Common, 61–90 Rare, 91–99 Epic and 100 Legendary. Rolls outside 1–100 are rejected. Each test case uses one roll. What is the minimum number of test cases for 100% equivalence partitioning coverage?
why: Six partitions: below 1 (invalid), 1–60, 61–90, 91–99, 100 (four valid), above 100 (invalid). One test per partition: 6.

distractorNotes.A: "One valid and one invalid test" ignores that each rarity is processed differently and that invalid values lie on both sides.
distractorNotes.B: Covers only the four valid partitions; invalid partitions count for EP coverage too.
distractorNotes.C: Forgets one of the two invalid partitions: rolls are rejected below 1 and above 100.

stem: The field-of-view setting accepts whole numbers from 60 to 110; any other number is rejected. Which is the SMALLEST set of test values that achieves 100% equivalence partitioning coverage?
why: Three partitions (59 and below, 60–110, 111 and above), one value each: 30, 85, 140.

distractorNotes.A: These are the 2-value BVA values. They do cover all three partitions, but with four values: not the smallest set.
distractorNotes.B: Misses the invalid partition below 60.
distractorNotes.D: All three values are in the valid partition; neither invalid partition is exercised.

stem: The matchmaking screen has three settings: region (EU, NA, Asia, OCE), mode (Solo, Duo, Squad) and crossplay (On, Off). Every value is valid and processed differently. What is the minimum number of test cases for 100% Each Choice coverage?
why: Each Choice needs every value of every setting at least once; combinations do not matter. The largest set (region) has 4 values, so 4 tests, e.g. (EU, Solo, On), (NA, Duo, Off), (Asia, Squad, On), (OCE, Solo, Off).

distractorNotes.A: 3 is the number of settings, not the size of the largest set of partitions.
distractorNotes.C: 9 adds the set sizes (4 + 3 + 2); one test can cover a value from each set at once.
distractorNotes.D: 24 is all combinations (4 × 3 × 2), which Each Choice coverage does not require.

stem: A jump-height setting moves in steps of 0.1. The spec: 1.0–2.4 is low, 2.5–3.9 medium, 4.0–5.0 high; values below 1.0 or above 5.0 are rejected. Tests use 0.5, 2.0, 3.0 and 3.5. What equivalence partitioning coverage do they achieve?
why: Five partitions: below 1.0, low, medium, high, above 5.0. Exercised: below 1.0 (0.5), low (2.0), medium (3.0 and 3.5): 3 of 5 = 60%.

distractorNotes.A: 2 of 5 forgets that 0.5 exercises the invalid partition below 1.0, which counts for EP coverage too.
distractorNotes.C: 3 of 4 forgets one of the two invalid partitions.
distractorNotes.D: 4 of 5 counts tests, not partitions: 3.0 and 3.5 are in the same partition.

stem: A race result function awards Gold for times under 60 s, Silver for 60–89 s, Bronze for 90–119 s and no medal for 120 s or more; negative times are rejected. Times are whole seconds. Tests so far use 45, 75 and 130. Which additional tests achieve 100% equivalence partitioning coverage with the fewest tests?
options: 100 only
59 and 60
why: Partitions: negative (invalid), 0–59 Gold, 60–89 Silver, 90–119 Bronze, 120+ no medal. 45, 75 and 130 cover Gold, Silver and no medal; still missing are Bronze (100) and negative (-5).

distractorNotes.B: Forgets the invalid partition of negative times.
distractorNotes.C: Boundary values from the Gold and Silver partitions, which are already covered.
distractorNotes.D: Achieves full coverage but not with the fewest tests: 150 is in the already covered no-medal partition.

stem: A tester writes these partitions for a stealth meter that goes from 0 to 100: 0–50 hidden, 50–80 suspicious, 80–100 detected. What is wrong with them?
options: There must be at least four valid partitions for a range of 101 values
Partitions must all contain the same number of values
Invalid partitions are only needed when the GDD gives them a name
The partitions overlap at 50 and 80, but each value must belong to exactly one partition
why: Partitions must not overlap: 50 and 80 each sit in two partitions, so the tester cannot know which behaviour to expect for them. The spec must say where 50 and 80 belong.

distractorNotes.A: The number of partitions comes from the different behaviours in the spec, not from the size of the range.
distractorNotes.B: Partitions can have any size, even one value.
distractorNotes.C: Values the spec does not process, or rejects, form invalid partitions whether or not the GDD names them.

stem: In the character creator the class can be Warrior, Mage or Rogue; each class starts with different gear. Any other class ID received from the server is rejected. How many equivalence partitions are there for the class?
why: Three valid partitions (each class is processed differently) plus one invalid partition (any other ID): 4.

distractorNotes.A: "Valid class" vs "invalid class" ignores that each class is processed differently.
distractorNotes.B: Forgets the invalid partition for unknown class IDs.
distractorNotes.D: An unordered set has no "below" and "above": there is one invalid partition, not two.

stem: A trading function has two inputs. Quantity: 1–99 valid, 0 or less and 100 or more invalid. Currency: Gold and Gems are valid and handled by different code; anything else is invalid. Each test case sets both inputs and may contain at most one invalid value. What is the minimum number of test cases to exercise every partition of both inputs at least once?
why: Quantity has 3 partitions, currency 3. The three invalid values each need their own test, and the valid partitions can ride along: (0, Gold), (150, Gems), (10, invalid currency). That covers all 6 partitions in 3 tests.

distractorNotes.B: No extra all-valid test is needed: the valid partitions are already covered next to the invalid values.
distractorNotes.C: 6 is the total number of partitions; one test covers a partition of each input.
distractorNotes.D: 9 is all combinations (3 × 3), more than every partition once requires.

stem: Tip dialog spec: a player may type a tip of 1 to 500 coins. A tip of 0 is also accepted and treated as "no tip" (the dialog closes without a transaction). Negative tips and tips over 500 are rejected. How many VALID equivalence partitions are there?
why: Two valid partitions: 0 (processed as "no tip") and 1–500 (a transaction). Negative and over 500 are the two invalid partitions.

distractorNotes.A: Range-based thinking: 0 is not in 1–500 but the spec defines how it is processed, so it is a valid partition of its own.
distractorNotes.C: Counts one of the rejected ranges as valid; rejected values are invalid.
distractorNotes.D: 4 is the total number of partitions, valid and invalid.

stem: The "max players" setting of a private lobby accepts 2 to 8; other numbers are rejected. A tester runs three tests with 1, 5 and 10. A reviewer says: "You never tested 2 and 8." Which statement is CORRECT?
options: EP coverage is only 33%, because just one value per partition was used
The tests do not count for EP coverage, because 1 and 10 are invalid
EP requires testing the minimum and the maximum of every partition
The tests achieve 100% EP coverage; 2 and 8 are boundary values that BVA would add
why: Three partitions (1 and below, 2–8, 9 and above), each exercised once: 100% EP coverage. Testing the edges of partitions is BVA.

distractorNotes.A: One value per partition is exactly what EP needs; coverage is partitions exercised over partitions identified.
distractorNotes.B: Invalid partitions are coverage items too; 1 and 10 exercise them.
distractorNotes.C: EP/BVA smear: minimum and maximum of each partition are the boundary values of BVA.

stem: A fishing rod's cast power is typed as a whole number. The game accepts 10 to 90 and rejects any other whole number. Which set of values achieves 100% 2-value boundary value analysis coverage?
why: Boundary values 10 and 90, each with its closest neighbour in the adjacent partition (9 and 91). 9 and 91 are also the boundary values of the invalid partitions, and their neighbours across are 10 and 90 again.

distractorNotes.A: Misses the neighbours in the adjacent invalid partitions.
distractorNotes.C: This is 3-value BVA for the boundaries 10 and 90.
distractorNotes.D: 0 and 100 are not neighbours of any boundary; 9 and 91 are.

stem: A respawn timer accepts whole seconds from 5 to 30; other whole numbers are rejected. Using 3-value boundary value analysis on the two boundary values of the valid partition (5 and 30), which test values are needed?
why: 3-value BVA takes each boundary value and both its neighbours: 5 → 4, 5, 6; 30 → 29, 30, 31.

distractorNotes.A: This is 2-value BVA: only the neighbour across the boundary.
distractorNotes.B: Only the inside neighbours; the neighbours in the invalid partitions (4 and 31) are missing.
distractorNotes.D: Shifted outwards: 3 and 32 are not neighbours of 5 or 30, and 6 and 29 are missing.

stem: Ammo capacity accepts whole numbers from 1 to 250; any other whole number is rejected. Which test value is used by 3-value boundary value analysis but NOT by 2-value boundary value analysis?
why: 2-value BVA uses 0, 1, 250, 251. 3-value BVA adds the inner neighbours of the boundary values, 2 and 249.

distractorNotes.A: 0 is the neighbour of 1 across the boundary: used by both variants.
distractorNotes.C: 251 is the neighbour of 250 across the boundary: used by both variants.
distractorNotes.D: 125 is a typical EP value from the middle of the valid partition, not a boundary neighbour.

stem: The armour rating slider only allows 0 to 100: 0–49 is light, 50–79 medium, 80–100 heavy. Which pair of values tests the boundary between light and medium with 2-value boundary value analysis?
options: 48 and 49
50 and 51
49 and 51
49 and 50
why: The boundary values on either side are 49 (max of light) and 50 (min of medium). Each one's closest neighbour in the adjacent partition is the other.

distractorNotes.A: Both values are in the light partition; the neighbour must come from the adjacent partition.
distractorNotes.B: Both values are in the medium partition.
distractorNotes.C: 51 is not a boundary value and not the neighbour of 49 across the boundary.

stem: A volume slider can only be set to whole numbers 0 to 10: 0 is muted, 1–7 normal, 8–10 shows a "loud" warning icon. How many coverage items does 2-value boundary value analysis have here?
why: Partitions {0}, {1–7}, {8–10}. Boundary values: 0, 1, 7, 8, 10. 2-value items: 0 and 1, 7 and 8, and 10 (no partition above it, because the slider cannot go higher). Distinct values: 0, 1, 7, 8, 10 = 5.

distractorNotes.A: Forgets that 10 is a boundary value too: it is the maximum of the 8–10 partition.
distractorNotes.C: Adds 11, which the slider cannot produce: there is no adjacent partition above 10.
distractorNotes.D: Counts 3-value style neighbours; 2-value takes only the boundary value and its neighbour across.

stem: A combo bonus must be given when the hit count is 10 or more. The developer writes the check as "hits == 10" instead of "hits >= 10". Partitions: 0–9 (no bonus) and 10 or more (bonus). Which test value reveals this defect AND is produced by 3-value but not by 2-value boundary value analysis?
why: 2-value BVA tests 9 and 10; both behave correctly with the faulty code. 3-value adds 11: the spec expects a bonus, the faulty code gives none.

distractorNotes.A: 9 is a 2-value value, and the faulty code correctly gives no bonus for it.
distractorNotes.B: 10 is a 2-value value, and the faulty code correctly gives a bonus for it.
distractorNotes.D: 12 would reveal the defect, but BVA does not produce it: it is not a neighbour of a boundary value.

stem: To which of these inputs can boundary value analysis NOT be applied?
options: The chosen character class: Warrior, Mage or Rogue
The player level, from 1 to 99
The size of a save file, up to 2 MB
The end date of a timed in-game event
why: BVA needs ordered partitions. A set of classes has no order, so it has no minimum or maximum.

distractorNotes.B: Levels are ordered numbers: classic BVA.
distractorNotes.C: File sizes are ordered: the 2 MB limit is a boundary.
distractorNotes.D: Dates are ordered too: the last day of the event and the day after are boundary tests.

stem: A sprint speed multiplier accepts values from 0.5 to 2.0 in steps of 0.1; anything else is rejected. Which set achieves 100% 2-value boundary value analysis coverage?
why: With a step of 0.1, the neighbour across each boundary is one step away: 0.4 next to 0.5, 2.1 next to 2.0.

distractorNotes.B: 0.49 and 2.01 cannot be entered: the step size is 0.1.
distractorNotes.C: 0 and 3.0 are invalid values but not the closest neighbours of the boundaries.
distractorNotes.D: All four values are in the valid partition; the neighbours must come from the adjacent invalid partitions.

stem: For a squad size field (2 to 6 valid; any other whole number can be typed and is rejected), the 2-value boundary value analysis coverage items are 1, 2, 6 and 7. The tests so far use 2, 4 and 7. What 2-value BVA coverage do they achieve?
why: Two of the four coverage items (2 and 7) are exercised: 50%. The value 4 is not a coverage item.

distractorNotes.A: Two items are exercised, not one.
distractorNotes.C: Counts 4 as covering an item; it is a middle value (an EP choice), not a boundary item.
distractorNotes.D: 1 and 6 are not exercised yet.

stem: Which defect is boundary value analysis MOST likely to find?
options: A crash caused by a missing texture on one rare enemy
A requirement for a photo mode that was never implemented
The wrong colour on the health bar
A check coded as "level > 10" where the spec says the perk unlocks from level 10 on
why: BVA targets boundaries placed one value too high or too low: here level 10 wrongly gets no perk.

distractorNotes.A: A missing asset has nothing to do with the edges of ordered partitions.
distractorNotes.B: A missing feature is not a boundary defect; no BVA test value would target it.
distractorNotes.C: A visual defect, not about values at the edge of a partition.

stem: An enemy's alert level is set by the game, never by the player, and is always 0 to 100: 0–39 unseen, 40–69 suspicious, 70–100 alerted. You apply 3-value boundary value analysis to the boundary values 39, 40, 69 and 70. How many distinct test values do you need?

distractorNotes.A: 4 is the 2-value count: the boundary values alone.
distractorNotes.B: Treats only 40 and 70 as boundary values; 39 and 69 are boundary values too.
distractorNotes.D: Three per boundary value without removing the duplicates (39, 40, 69, 70 appear twice).

stem: A limited-entry decision table has four Boolean conditions, and every combination is feasible. How many columns does the full table have?
why: Each Boolean condition doubles the number of combinations: 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 16 columns.

distractorNotes.A: One column per condition is not how decision rules work; each column is a combination.
distractorNotes.B: 8 is the count for three conditions.
distractorNotes.D: 32 is the count for five conditions.

stem: A matchmaking rule has three Boolean conditions: C1 "player level below 10", C2 "player level 50 or above", C3 "player is in a party". How many feasible columns does the full limited-entry decision table have?
why: The full table has 8 columns. C1 and C2 can never both be true, which makes 2 columns infeasible (C3 true and C3 false): 8 − 2 = 6.

distractorNotes.A: Counts the infeasible columns, which are not coverage items.
distractorNotes.B: Removes only one column; the impossible C1/C2 combination appears twice, once for each value of C3.
distractorNotes.D: Removes too many: only the combination C1 true and C2 true is impossible.

stem: A daily login reward has this decision table. R1: logged in yesterday T, VIP T → 3× reward and badge. R2: T, F → 2× reward. R3: F, T → 1× reward and badge. R4: F, F → 1× reward. Tests: T1 (logged in yesterday, not VIP), T2 (not yesterday, not VIP), T3 (logged in yesterday, not VIP). What decision table coverage do the tests achieve?
why: T1 and T3 both exercise R2; T2 exercises R4. Two of the four columns: 50%.

distractorNotes.A: R1 and R3 (VIP players) are never exercised.
distractorNotes.B: Counts T3 as a new column; it repeats R2.
distractorNotes.D: Two different columns are exercised, not one.

stem: A vault door's rules use three conditions. R1: has key T, boss defeated T, hard mode – → open the vault. R2: has key T, boss defeated F, hard mode T → show "Defeat the boss". R3: has key F, boss defeated –, hard mode – → show "Find the key". Which combination of conditions is covered by NO rule, showing a gap in the requirements?
options: Has key F, boss defeated T, hard mode T
Has key T, boss defeated T, hard mode F
Has key T, boss defeated F, hard mode F
Has key F, boss defeated F, hard mode F
why: R1 covers key T, boss T (any mode); R3 covers every key F combination; R2 covers key T, boss F only in hard mode. Key T, boss F, hard mode F has no rule.

distractorNotes.A: Covered by R3: with no key, boss and mode do not matter.
distractorNotes.B: Covered by R1: hard mode does not matter when the key is held and the boss is defeated.
distractorNotes.D: Covered by R3.

stem: Store discount rules: a first purchase always gets 50% off. Otherwise, bundles get 20% off; non-bundle items get 10% off on sale weekends, and no discount at other times. After merging the columns in which a condition does not affect the outcome, how many test cases are needed for 100% decision table coverage?
why: Conditions: first purchase, bundle, sale weekend. Merged rules: (T, –, –) 50%; (F, T, –) 20%; (F, F, T) 10%; (F, F, F) none. Four columns, four tests.

distractorNotes.A: Merges too far: the sale-weekend and normal non-bundle cases have different outcomes.
distractorNotes.C: Merges too little: the four first-purchase columns become one column and the two bundle columns another, which leaves 4, not 6.
distractorNotes.D: 8 is the full, unmerged table with three conditions.

stem: An extended-entry decision table for loot drops has two conditions: enemy type (Normal, Elite, Boss) and difficulty (Easy, Normal, Hard, Nightmare). Every combination is feasible and gives a different drop. How many columns does the table have?
why: In an extended-entry table, multiply the numbers of values: 3 × 4 = 12 combinations, so 12 columns.

distractorNotes.A: Adds the numbers of values (3 + 4); columns are combinations.
distractorNotes.C: Treats both conditions as if they had four values each.
distractorNotes.D: Treats each of the 7 values as a separate Boolean condition (2 to the power 7).

stem: In a limited-entry decision table, what does a "–" in a condition cell of a column mean?
options: The combination is infeasible and needs no test
The action in that column is not carried out
The designers have not decided the value yet
The condition's value does not affect the outcome of that rule
why: "–" marks a condition that is irrelevant for that rule, typically after merging columns. The column is still a coverage item.

distractorNotes.A: Infeasible combinations are marked N/A, not "–".
distractorNotes.B: Actions are marked with X (happens) or left blank (does not happen); "–" is about conditions.
distractorNotes.C: An undecided value would be a gap or defect in the requirements, not a table notation.

stem: Log-in rules for an online game. R1: account banned T, maintenance –, premium – → show ban screen. R2: banned F, maintenance T, premium T → priority queue. R3: banned F, maintenance T, premium F → maintenance message. R4: banned F, maintenance F, premium – → log in. Tests: T1 (banned F, maintenance T, premium F), T2 (banned T, maintenance F, premium T), T3 (banned F, maintenance F, premium T). Which additional test achieves 100% decision table coverage?
options: Banned F, maintenance T, premium T
Banned T, maintenance T, premium T
Banned F, maintenance F, premium F
Banned F, maintenance T, premium F
why: T1 covers R3, T2 covers R1, T3 covers R4. Only R2 (not banned, maintenance, premium) is missing.

distractorNotes.B: Banned T falls under R1, which T2 already covers.
distractorNotes.C: Falls under R4, which T3 already covers.
distractorNotes.D: Repeats R3, the rule T1 already covers.

stem: A team wants to test a crafting rule with seven Boolean conditions using a decision table. Which concern is MOST relevant?
options: The full table has 128 columns, so the team may use a minimised table or a risk-based selection of rules
Decision tables cannot handle more than three conditions
Decision tables only work for numeric inputs
Columns may never be merged, so the team needs exactly seven test cases
why: The number of columns grows exponentially (2 to the power 7 = 128). Minimising the table or selecting rules by risk keeps the effort manageable.

distractorNotes.B: There is no such limit; the size just grows quickly.
distractorNotes.C: Decision tables are for combinations of conditions, most often Boolean ones.
distractorNotes.D: Columns can be merged where a condition does not affect the outcome; and the count is not one per condition.

stem: A full limited-entry decision table has three Boolean conditions. Two of its columns are infeasible. The tests exercise three different feasible columns. What decision table coverage do they achieve?
why: 8 columns − 2 infeasible = 6 coverage items. 3 of 6 exercised = 50%.

distractorNotes.A: Divides by all 8 columns; infeasible columns are not coverage items.
distractorNotes.C: Divides by 5, as if three columns were infeasible.
distractorNotes.D: Overgeneralisation: three of the six feasible columns are still untested.

stem: Which coverage criterion is fully achieved when every state of the model has been visited at least once?
options: Valid transitions coverage
All transitions coverage
All states coverage
0-switch coverage
why: All states coverage has the states as coverage items: 100% when every state has been visited.

distractorNotes.A: Valid transitions coverage needs every valid transition exercised, which visiting the states does not guarantee.
distractorNotes.B: All transitions coverage also needs every invalid transition attempted.
distractorNotes.D: 0-switch coverage is another name for valid transitions coverage.

stem: A guard NPC has this model. Idle → Chase on "sees player"; Idle → Patrol on "timer"; Patrol → Idle on "timer"; Patrol → Chase on "sees player"; Chase → Attack on "in range"; Attack → Chase on "out of range"; Chase → Patrol on "loses player". How many coverage items does valid transitions coverage have?
why: The coverage items are the valid transitions: there are 7 in the model.

distractorNotes.A: 4 is the number of states: the coverage items of all states coverage.
distractorNotes.B: Off by one: count each arrow, including both "timer" transitions.
distractorNotes.D: 20 is the number of cells of the state table (4 states × 5 events): the coverage items of all transitions coverage.

stem: A quest has this model. Locked → Available on "reach level 5"; Available → Active on "accept"; Active → Available on "abandon"; Active → Completed on "complete objective"; Active → Failed on "timer expires"; Failed → Active on "retry". Completed has no outgoing transitions. Every test case starts in Locked. What is the minimum number of test cases for 100% valid transitions coverage?
why: One sequence covers all six: reach level 5, accept, abandon, accept, timer expires, retry, complete objective (Locked → Available → Active → Available → Active → Failed → Active → Completed).

distractorNotes.B: Failed is not a final state: "retry" leads back to Active, so one test can continue to Completed.
distractorNotes.C: No transition forces a separate test; one sequence can chain them all.
distractorNotes.D: One test per transition ignores that a test case usually covers several transitions.

stem: A download manager has this model. Queued → Downloading on "start"; Downloading → Paused on "pause"; Paused → Downloading on "resume"; Downloading → Installed on "finish"; Downloading → Failed on "error"; Queued → Cancelled on "cancel". Installed, Failed and Cancelled are final states. Every test case starts in Queued and ends in a final state. What is the minimum number of test cases for 100% valid transitions coverage?
why: Three transitions lead into final states (finish, error, cancel), and a test case can end in only one of them: at least 3. Three suffice: start, pause, resume, finish; start, error; cancel.

distractorNotes.A: Two test cases can reach only two of the three final states.
distractorNotes.C: The pause/resume loop fits into one of the three test cases; no fourth is needed.
distractorNotes.D: One test per transition ignores that test cases chain transitions.

stem: The state model of a weapon has 5 states and 8 valid transitions. The test cases visited all 5 states and exercised 6 different valid transitions. What valid transitions coverage do they achieve?
why: Valid transitions coverage = exercised valid transitions ÷ valid transitions: 6 ÷ 8 = 75%.

distractorNotes.A: Divides 6 by 10, a number that is in the model nowhere.
distractorNotes.B: 5 ÷ 8 mixes the number of states with the number of transitions.
distractorNotes.D: 100% is the all states coverage; visiting every state does not exercise every transition.

stem: Which statement about state transition coverage criteria is CORRECT?
options: 100% all states coverage guarantees 100% valid transitions coverage
Valid transitions coverage requires attempting every invalid transition
All transitions coverage is reached when every state has been entered and left once
100% valid transitions coverage guarantees 100% all states coverage
why: Exercising every valid transition means entering every state, so full valid transitions coverage guarantees full all states coverage. The reverse is not true.

distractorNotes.A: The wrong way round: states can all be visited while some transitions are never exercised.
distractorNotes.B: Attempting invalid transitions belongs to all transitions coverage.
distractorNotes.C: Entering and leaving each state once neither exercises every valid transition nor attempts the invalid ones.

stem: A platform elevator has this model, starting in Down. Down → MovingUp on "button"; MovingUp → Up on "arrive"; Up → MovingDown on "button"; MovingDown → Down on "arrive"; MovingUp → MovingDown on "obstacle". Which event sequence achieves 100% valid transitions coverage?
options: button, obstacle, arrive, button, arrive, button, arrive
button, arrive, button, arrive
button, obstacle, arrive, button, arrive
button, arrive, obstacle, arrive
why: Down → MovingUp (button) → MovingDown (obstacle) → Down (arrive) → MovingUp (button) → Up (arrive) → MovingDown (button) → Down (arrive): all 5 valid transitions.

distractorNotes.B: Never exercises the obstacle transition: 4 of 5.
distractorNotes.C: Ends in Up, so Up → MovingDown is never exercised: 4 of 5.
distractorNotes.D: "obstacle" in state Up is an invalid transition; the sequence also misses MovingUp → MovingDown.

stem: The state table of a lock-on targeting system has 4 states and 5 events (no guard conditions). 7 of its cells contain valid transitions. How many invalid transitions must be attempted for 100% all transitions coverage?
why: The table has 4 × 5 = 20 cells; the 20 − 7 = 13 empty cells are the invalid transitions.

distractorNotes.A: 7 is the number of valid transitions.
distractorNotes.C: 20 is all the cells: the coverage items of all transitions coverage, valid ones included.
distractorNotes.D: Adds the valid transitions to the cells instead of subtracting them.

stem: A character's jump has this model. Grounded → Airborne on "jump [stamina ≥ 10] / play jump sound"; Grounded → Grounded on "jump [stamina < 10] / show tired icon"; Airborne → Grounded on "land"; Airborne → DoubleJumping on "double jump [has double jump]"; DoubleJumping → Grounded on "land". How many coverage items does valid transitions coverage have?
why: Five valid transitions: the two guarded "jump" transitions are separate, including the self-transition, plus the two "land" transitions and the double jump.

distractorNotes.A: 3 is the number of states.
distractorNotes.B: Forgets the self-transition Grounded → Grounded: it is a valid transition and a coverage item.
distractorNotes.D: Counts the actions or guards as extra items; each arrow is one transition.

stem: For all transitions coverage, a tester puts only one invalid transition in each test case. What is the main reason?
options: Invalid transitions can only be tested at the end of a test case
To reach 100% all states coverage faster
The state table allows only one empty cell per row
To avoid fault masking, where one defect hides another
why: If several invalid transitions are in one test case, the reaction to the first can hide a defect in the handling of the next: fault masking.

distractorNotes.A: No such rule; the point is not their position but their number.
distractorNotes.B: Invalid transitions add nothing to all states coverage.
distractorNotes.C: A row can have many empty cells; each is an invalid transition.

stem: A save system has this model, starting in Idle. Idle → Saving on "save"; Saving → Idle on "done"; Saving → Error on "disk full"; Error → Saving on "retry"; Error → Idle on "cancel"; Idle → Loading on "load"; Loading → Idle on "done". One test case: save, disk full, retry, done. What valid transitions coverage does it achieve (rounded)?
why: It exercises Idle → Saving, Saving → Error, Error → Saving and Saving → Idle: 4 of 7 valid transitions = 57%.

distractorNotes.A: 3 of 7: the repeated Saving state still leads to a new transition (done to Idle).
distractorNotes.C: 3 of 4 is the all states coverage (Loading is never visited), not transitions.
distractorNotes.D: The cancel, load and Loading → Idle transitions are never exercised.

stem: In statement testing, what are the coverage items?
options: The decision outcomes in the code
The requirements the code implements
The paths through the control flow graph
The executable statements
why: Statement testing exercises the executable statements; coverage is measured as the share of executable statements that ran.

distractorNotes.A: Decision outcomes (conditional branches) are coverage items of branch testing.
distractorNotes.B: Requirements are the basis of black-box testing, not white-box coverage items.
distractorNotes.C: Paths are not the coverage items of either technique in the syllabus.

stem: Treat each numbered line as one executable statement: 1 bonus = 0; 2 if (streak > 5); 3 bonus = 50; 4 score = score + bonus. One test runs with streak = 3. What statement coverage does it achieve?
why: With streak = 3 the condition is false, so statements 1, 2 and 4 run and 3 does not: 3 of 4 = 75%.

distractorNotes.A: Only one statement would be 25%; three statements run.
distractorNotes.B: The if statement itself (line 2) is executed and counts.
distractorNotes.D: Line 3 never runs, because streak = 3 does not satisfy streak > 5.

stem: A method contains: if (isNight) { SpawnWolves(); } else { SpawnDeer(); } followed by if (isRaining) { PlayRain(); }. What is the minimum number of test cases for 100% statement coverage?
why: SpawnWolves and SpawnDeer are on opposite sides of one decision, so two tests are needed. PlayRain can run in either of them (isRaining true).

distractorNotes.A: One test can never run both the if part and the else part of the same decision.
distractorNotes.C: The second if has no else, so it needs no test of its own: its statement runs alongside one of the two tests.
distractorNotes.D: 4 is the number of combinations of the two conditions, more than statement coverage needs.

stem: Which statement about 100% statement coverage is CORRECT?
options: Every decision outcome in the code has been tested
There are no defects left in the code
It guarantees 100% branch coverage
Every executable statement has run at least once, but defects that depend on particular data values may still be missed
why: 100% statement coverage means each executable statement ran at least once. A statement can run without failing, e.g. a division that only fails when the divisor is 0.

distractorNotes.A: An if without an else can be fully covered without its false outcome: decision outcomes are branch coverage.
distractorNotes.B: Overgeneralisation: testing shows the presence of defects, not their absence.
distractorNotes.C: The wrong way round: branch coverage subsumes statement coverage, not the reverse.

stem: A results screen computes ratio = kills / deaths. The only test uses deaths = 4, and the test suite reaches 100% statement coverage of the method. After release, the screen crashes for players with no deaths. Why did statement testing not find this?
options: The test suite was in fact below 100% statement coverage
A division is not an executable statement, so it was never measured
Exercising a statement once does not reveal defects that only appear with certain data values
Statement testing only checks that the code compiles
why: The division ran (so it counts as covered) but only with a non-zero value. The crash depends on the data (deaths = 0), which statement coverage does not ask for.

distractorNotes.A: The stem says the coverage was 100%; the gap is in the data, not in the coverage.
distractorNotes.B: An assignment with a division is an executable statement.
distractorNotes.D: Statement testing executes the code; compiling is not testing.

stem: A script has 20 executable statements. Test T1 runs 12 of them. Test T2 runs 10, of which 6 were also run by T1. What statement coverage do T1 and T2 achieve together?
why: Distinct statements run: 12 + 10 − 6 = 16. 16 of 20 = 80%.

distractorNotes.A: T2's 10 statements alone would be 50%; the two tests together run more.
distractorNotes.B: T1's 12 statements alone are 60%; T2 adds 4 new ones.
distractorNotes.D: Adds 12 + 10 without removing the 6 statements run by both tests.

stem: A coverage report shows that the else block of a damage method has never run; everything else has. Which new test is the best way to increase statement coverage?
options: Repeat the existing tests with more test data from the same partitions
A review of the method's comments
A test of a different method that has lower coverage
A test whose input makes the if condition false
why: The else block only runs when the if condition is false; a test with such an input executes the missing statements.

distractorNotes.A: More values that take the same route through the code add no new statements.
distractorNotes.B: Comments are not executable statements, and a review is static testing.
distractorNotes.C: Improves another method's coverage, not this method's missing else block.

stem: In branch testing, what is a branch?
options: A transfer of control between two nodes of the control flow graph, either unconditional or conditional
A copy of the code base in version control
Only the true outcome of an if statement
A complete path from the start of a method to its end
why: A branch is a transfer of control between two nodes of the control flow graph. Unconditional branches are straight-line code; conditional ones are decision outcomes.

distractorNotes.B: A version-control branch is a configuration management term, not a coverage item.
distractorNotes.C: Both outcomes of a decision are branches, and so is straight-line code.
distractorNotes.D: A full path combines many branches; paths are not the coverage items of branch testing.

stem: Which statement about statement coverage and branch coverage is CORRECT?
options: 100% branch coverage guarantees 100% statement coverage, but not the other way round
100% statement coverage guarantees 100% branch coverage
The two criteria always give the same percentage
Branch coverage only counts the conditional branches, so it is weaker than statement coverage
why: Branch coverage subsumes statement coverage: exercising every branch runs every statement. An if without an else shows the reverse is not true.

distractorNotes.B: The wrong way round: one test can run every statement and still skip a false outcome.
distractorNotes.C: They are measured on different coverage items and often differ.
distractorNotes.D: Unconditional branches count too, and branch coverage is the stronger criterion.

stem: Code: if (ammo == 0) { Reload(); } Fire(); What is the minimum number of test cases for 100% branch coverage?
why: The decision has two outcomes: ammo == 0 true (Reload, then Fire) and false (straight to Fire). Each needs a test: 2.

distractorNotes.A: One test (ammo = 0) gives 100% statement coverage, but the false outcome is never taken.
distractorNotes.C: Only one decision with two outcomes; Fire() runs in both tests.
distractorNotes.D: There is only one condition, so there are not four combinations.

stem: Code: if (inWater) { if (hasGills) { Breathe(); } else { Drown(); } } else { Walk(); }. What is the minimum number of test cases for 100% branch coverage?
why: Three routes: inWater true and hasGills true (Breathe), inWater true and hasGills false (Drown), inWater false (Walk). They cover all four decision outcomes; no two of them can be merged.

distractorNotes.A: Two tests can cover at most two of the three blocks Breathe, Drown and Walk.
distractorNotes.C: Four would be all combinations of the two conditions, but hasGills is only checked when inWater is true.
distractorNotes.D: 6 counts every branch, not the tests needed; one test exercises several branches.

stem: Code: while (enemiesLeft > 0) { SpawnNext(); enemiesLeft--; } EndWave(); What is the minimum number of test cases for 100% branch coverage?
options: Branch coverage cannot be measured for loops
why: One test starting with, say, 2 enemies enters the loop (decision true), loops back, and finally leaves it (decision false): both outcomes and all other branches in one test.

distractorNotes.B: A second test with 0 enemies takes the false outcome again, which the first test already exercised when the loop ended.
distractorNotes.C: There is only one decision; one well-chosen test exercises both its outcomes.
distractorNotes.D: Staying in or leaving a loop are conditional branches like any other.

stem: The control flow graph of a reload method has 10 branches. The tests exercise 6 of them. Which statement is CORRECT?
options: Branch coverage is 60%, and statement coverage is also exactly 60%
Branch coverage is 40%
Branch coverage is 60%; the statement coverage cannot be worked out from this information
Branch coverage is 60%, so statement coverage must be 100%
why: 6 of 10 branches = 60%. The two criteria count different items, so the branch figure alone does not give the statement coverage.

distractorNotes.A: Statements and branches are different coverage items; their percentages usually differ.
distractorNotes.B: 40% is the share of branches not exercised.
distractorNotes.D: Only 100% branch coverage guarantees 100% statement coverage.

stem: Code: if (hp < 30) { ShowWarning(); } if (hp == 0) { GameOver(); }. Which set of test inputs achieves 100% branch coverage?
options: hp = 10 and hp = 50
hp = 0 and hp = 10
hp = 0 only
hp = 0 and hp = 50
why: hp = 0 takes both decisions true; hp = 50 takes both false. All four decision outcomes are exercised.

distractorNotes.A: hp == 0 is never true, so GameOver's branch is never taken.
distractorNotes.B: hp < 30 is never false.
distractorNotes.C: Gives 100% statement coverage, but neither false outcome is taken.

stem: What is the fundamental strength of white-box testing?
options: It takes the whole implementation into account, so defects can be found even when the specification is vague, outdated or incomplete
It finds requirements that were never implemented
It needs no knowledge of the code, so anyone can do it
It proves that the software meets the users' needs
why: Because white-box testing works on the actual implementation, it can find defects even where the specification is poor.

distractorNotes.B: The opposite: unimplemented requirements (defects of omission) are its weakness.
distractorNotes.C: White-box techniques are based on the internal structure, so knowledge of the code is needed.
distractorNotes.D: Overgeneralisation: no testing proves that; meeting users' needs is a validation question.

stem: The GDD says that kills during a double-XP weekend earn twice the XP. The developer never implemented it. The XP code has 100% branch coverage and all its tests pass. Why did white-box testing not reveal the problem?
options: The branch coverage figure must have been wrong
The tests should have been run with more data from the same partitions
Branch testing only finds defects in loops
White-box testing cannot find defects of omission: there is no code for the missing requirement to cover
why: Coverage measures the code that exists. A requirement that was never implemented leaves no code, so no white-box criterion points at it; a black-box test from the GDD would.

distractorNotes.A: The coverage can be truly 100%: all the code that exists was exercised.
distractorNotes.B: More values through the same code still never reach code that does not exist.
distractorNotes.C: Branch testing covers all decisions, not only loops; the real issue is the missing code.

stem: Which statement about white-box techniques is CORRECT?
options: They can be used in static testing, e.g. a dry run of pseudocode that is not yet ready to execute
They can only be applied while the code is being executed
They are only useful when the specification is complete
They replace the need for black-box testing at the component level
why: White-box techniques also help in static testing: dry runs of code not ready to run, and reviews of pseudocode or other logic that can be modelled as a control flow graph.

distractorNotes.B: They can also be applied statically, without executing anything.
distractorNotes.C: One of their strengths is that they work when the specification is poor.
distractorNotes.D: Overgeneralisation: black-box tests are still needed, e.g. for missing requirements.

stem: A team tests a new physics module with black-box techniques only. What important information do they NOT get?
options: Whether the module meets its requirements
Which failures occur when the module is used as the players would
Whether the module's specified boundaries are handled correctly
A measure of how much of the actual code the tests exercised
why: Black-box testing alone gives no measure of actual code coverage; white-box coverage measures provide it.

distractorNotes.A: Checking the requirements is exactly what black-box tests do.
distractorNotes.B: Black-box tests run the module and can show such failures.
distractorNotes.C: BVA is a black-box technique, so the boundaries are tested.

stem: Which of the following is NOT a benefit of white-box coverage measures?
options: They give an objective measurement of coverage
They show where extra tests are needed to increase coverage
They show that every requirement has been implemented
They help increase confidence in the code
why: Coverage only describes the code that exists; it cannot show that every requirement was implemented (defects of omission).

distractorNotes.A: An objective coverage figure is a real benefit.
distractorNotes.B: Coverage reports point at untested code, so extra tests can be designed.
distractorNotes.D: Higher coverage gives more confidence in the code.

stem: A studio inherits a modding plugin from a contractor. Its only documentation is a two-page readme from three versions ago, but the source code is complete. Which approach is MOST likely to find defects in the plugin's actual behaviour?
options: White-box tests designed from the source code, with coverage measured
Black-box tests derived only from the outdated readme
Waiting until a new specification is written before testing
Checklist-based testing with a checklist built from the readme
why: White-box testing takes the whole implementation into account, so it can find defects even when the specification is outdated or incomplete.

distractorNotes.B: Tests from an outdated spec miss everything the readme no longer describes.
distractorNotes.C: Delays testing for no reason; the code itself can be the basis now.
distractorNotes.D: A checklist built from the same outdated readme inherits its gaps.

stem: Before a release, a tester lists the defects developers made in the studio's last three titles (off-by-one errors in inventory slots, missing null checks on optional DLC assets) and designs a test to expose each one. Which technique is this?
options: Exploratory testing
Checklist-based testing
Error anticipation testing
A fault attack, the methodical form of error guessing
why: A list of possible defects, built from experience, with tests designed to expose each one, is a fault attack: methodical error guessing.

distractorNotes.A: Exploratory testing designs tests while learning about the test object; here the tests come from a prepared defect list.
distractorNotes.B: A checklist holds test conditions to cover; this is a list of likely defects to expose.
distractorNotes.C: Informal paraphrase: "error anticipation" is not a syllabus term. The technique is error guessing.

stem: Error guessing is based on the tester's knowledge. Which of the following is NOT a typical source of that knowledge?
options: How the application has worked in the past
The kinds of errors developers tend to make
The decision outcomes in the control flow graph of the code
Failures that occurred in other, similar applications
why: Decision outcomes in the control flow graph are the basis of white-box branch testing, not of error guessing.

distractorNotes.A: Past behaviour of the application is a classic source for error guessing.
distractorNotes.B: Knowing the errors developers tend to make is a classic source.
distractorNotes.D: Failures in similar applications are a classic source.

stem: A tester suspects that the developer forgot to reset the combo counter to zero at the start of each round. In which area of typical errors does this guess fall?
options: Input
Output
Interfaces
Data
why: A wrong or missing initialisation is a data error.

distractorNotes.A: Input errors are about correct inputs not accepted or parameters wrong or missing.
distractorNotes.B: Output errors are about wrong formats or wrong results being shown.
distractorNotes.C: Interface errors are about mismatched parameters or incompatible types between parts.

stem: Which statement about fault attacks is CORRECT?
options: They are random inputs given to the game to see what happens
They are another name for exploratory testing sessions
They need a formal specification from which the attacks are derived
They need a list of possible errors, defects and failures, which can come from experience, defect and failure data, or common knowledge about why software fails
why: Fault attacks are the methodical form of error guessing: the tester creates or acquires a list of possible errors, defects and failures and designs tests for them.

distractorNotes.A: Random inputs have no defect list behind them; fault attacks are targeted.
distractorNotes.B: Exploratory testing is a separate experience-based technique, driven by learning.
distractorNotes.C: The list comes from experience and data, not from a formal specification.

stem: On a new racing game, a senior tester sets up a lap longer than 10 minutes, because a similar title she tested showed the lap timer jumping from 9:59 to 0:00. Which technique is she using?
options: Error guessing
Exploratory testing
Checklist-based testing
State transition testing
why: She anticipates a failure from failures seen in a similar application: error guessing.

distractorNotes.B: Her test was chosen before the session from past experience, not while learning about this game.
distractorNotes.C: There is no checklist of test conditions here.
distractorNotes.D: No state model of the timer is being used.

stem: Match each guessed defect (1–4) with its area (a–d). 1. A valid gamer tag is refused; 2. Health is displayed as 1.0E2; 3. AND was used where the rule needs OR; 4. Two modules disagree on the type of the score parameter. a. Logic; b. Interfaces; c. Input; d. Output.
why: A correct input not accepted is input; a wrong display format is output; a wrong operator is logic; a parameter type mismatch is interfaces.

distractorNotes.B: Swaps input and output: a refused tag is an input error, a wrong number format an output error.
distractorNotes.C: Swaps logic and interfaces: AND/OR is a logic error, type mismatch an interface error.
distractorNotes.D: Swaps output and logic: the 1.0E2 display is an output format error.

stem: What does the syllabus call the methodical approach to implementing error guessing?
options: Fault attacks
Defect clustering
Error seeding
Attack-based checklists
why: Fault attacks are the methodical way to implement error guessing.

distractorNotes.B: Defect clustering is a testing principle about defects concentrating in a few modules.
distractorNotes.C: Error seeding (inserting known defects) is not this technique.
distractorNotes.D: Invented term that mixes two techniques; checklists belong to checklist-based testing.

stem: Which statement about error guessing is CORRECT?
options: It needs a formal specification to derive the tests
It is the same as exploratory testing, because tests are designed during execution
It anticipates errors, defects and failures from the tester's knowledge, such as the errors developers tend to make
It gives an objective coverage measure of the code
why: Error guessing uses the tester's knowledge of past behaviour, typical developer errors and failures of similar applications to anticipate problems.

distractorNotes.A: Error guessing is experience-based; a formal specification is the basis of black-box techniques.
distractorNotes.B: Adjacent-concept swap: designing during execution while learning is exploratory testing.
distractorNotes.D: Objective code coverage comes from white-box techniques.

stem: Which statement BEST describes exploratory testing?
options: Testing without any plan, guided only by the tester's instinct
Tests are designed from the code until every branch is covered
Tests are designed in advance from a checklist and executed later
Tests are designed, executed and evaluated at the same time, while the tester learns about the test object
why: The defining trait: test design, execution and evaluation happen simultaneously, driven by what the tester learns.

distractorNotes.A: Informal paraphrase: the exam idea is learning, not instinct, and session-based testing gives it structure.
distractorNotes.B: Designing tests from the code is white-box branch testing.
distractorNotes.C: Designing tests in advance from a checklist is checklist-based testing.

stem: Which set of elements belongs to session-based exploratory testing?
options: A time-box, a test charter with test objectives, and a debriefing afterwards
A fixed test script, expected results and a pass/fail log
A list of likely defects and a test for each of them
A control flow graph and a coverage report
why: Session-based testing runs exploratory testing within a time-box, guided by a charter with test objectives, followed by a debriefing (with session sheets to note what happened).

distractorNotes.B: Fixed scripts with expected results are scripted testing, the opposite of exploratory.
distractorNotes.C: A defect list with tests for each item is a fault attack (error guessing).
distractorNotes.D: Control flow graphs and coverage reports belong to white-box testing.

stem: In which situation is exploratory testing MOST useful?
options: The specification is thin and the release date leaves little time for testing
The regulator requires scripted, repeatable test evidence
A complete, detailed specification exists and every test case is already written
The team needs an objective measure of code coverage
why: Exploratory testing is most useful when specifications are few or inadequate, or when there is significant time pressure.

distractorNotes.B: Repeatable scripted evidence calls for scripted tests; exploratory sessions vary by nature.
distractorNotes.C: It can complement such testing, but this is not where it is most useful.
distractorNotes.D: Objective code coverage comes from white-box techniques.

stem: A tester receives a new fishing mini-game build with no documentation. For 60 minutes she follows a charter, "Explore line tension to find ways to break the reel", notes her steps and findings on a sheet, and afterwards talks the results through with the lead. Which technique is this?
options: Checklist-based testing
A fault attack
Exploration testing
Session-based exploratory testing
why: Time-box, charter, session sheet and debriefing are the elements of session-based exploratory testing.

distractorNotes.A: A charter with objectives is not a checklist of test conditions.
distractorNotes.B: A fault attack starts from a list of likely defects; here the tester learns as she goes.
distractorNotes.C: Informal paraphrase: "exploration testing" is not a syllabus term; the term is exploratory testing.

stem: Which statement about exploratory testing is NOT correct?
options: It is more effective when the tester is experienced, has domain knowledge, and is analytical, curious and creative
The test objectives in a charter can be treated as high-level test conditions
It cannot make use of other test techniques such as equivalence partitioning
It is useful as a complement to more formal test techniques
why: Exploratory testing can incorporate other techniques; a tester can apply EP to a field she discovers during the session.

distractorNotes.A: True: these skills make exploratory testing more effective.
distractorNotes.B: True: the charter's objectives act as high-level test conditions.
distractorNotes.D: True: it complements more formal techniques.

stem: In session-based exploratory testing, what usually happens right after a test session?
options: The test charter for the session is written
The session is repeated with test automation to confirm the results
The test completion report for the project is written
A debriefing, where the tester and interested stakeholders discuss the results
why: A session is usually followed by a debriefing between the tester and the stakeholders interested in the results.

distractorNotes.A: The charter guides the session, so it exists before the session starts.
distractorNotes.B: Nothing in session-based testing requires repeating a session with automation.
distractorNotes.C: The test completion report belongs to test completion at the end of the project or iteration.

stem: In session-based exploratory testing, what is a test session sheet used for?
options: To document the steps followed and the discoveries made during the session
To list the expected results of each test step before the session
To record the time-box agreed in the project's test plan
To list the exit criteria that end the test level
why: Test session sheets record what the tester did and what they discovered.

distractorNotes.B: Expected results written in advance belong to scripted test cases.
distractorNotes.C: The time-box is part of the session set-up; the sheet records the session's steps and findings.
distractorNotes.D: Exit criteria belong to test planning, not to a session sheet.

stem: An hour into testing the new co-op lobby, a tester notices that party invites expire after about five minutes. She spends the rest of the session sending invites just before and after that time and while players change region. Which technique BEST describes what she is doing?
options: Checklist-based testing
Decision table testing
A fault attack
Exploratory testing
why: She uses what she has just learned about the lobby to design her next tests, running and evaluating them at once: exploratory testing.

distractorNotes.A: No checklist of test conditions is involved.
distractorNotes.B: No combinations of conditions are being tabulated from a specification.
distractorNotes.C: There is no prepared list of likely defects; the idea comes from what she observed.

stem: A team is drafting a checklist for testing a settings menu. Which item should NOT be on it?
options: Does each setting keep its value after the game is restarted?
Can every setting be changed with a gamepad alone?
Did the build pass all automated unit tests?
Is the text of each setting readable at the smallest font size?
why: Items that can be checked automatically do not belong on a checklist; the CI pipeline already reports the unit test results.

distractorNotes.A: A specific test condition, phrased as a question and checkable directly: a good item.
distractorNotes.B: A good item: specific and checkable.
distractorNotes.D: A good item about a quality characteristic (usability).

stem: Which of these items is better suited as an exit criterion than as a checklist item?
options: All critical and high-severity defects are closed
Does the subtitle language change when the system language changes?
Does the game pause when the controller is disconnected?
Is the controller layout screen readable on a 7-inch handheld screen?
why: "All critical defects closed" is a condition for ending testing: an exit criterion. Checklists should not hold items better used as entry or exit criteria.

distractorNotes.B: A specific, checkable test condition: a good checklist item.
distractorNotes.C: A specific, checkable test condition: a good checklist item.
distractorNotes.D: A specific usability check: a good checklist item.

stem: Which checklist item is badly written?
options: Is the game fun?
Does every tutorial prompt show the button of the connected controller?
Can the player skip each cutscene?
Does the inventory show a message when it is full?
why: Too general to check separately and directly; checklist items should be specific.

distractorNotes.B: Specific and checkable.
distractorNotes.C: Specific and checkable.
distractorNotes.D: Specific and checkable.

stem: Which statement about maintaining a test checklist is CORRECT?
options: Once written, a checklist should stay unchanged so results remain comparable
Items only lose value when the product's requirements change
Items should be added for every defect found, of any severity
It should be updated regularly from defect analysis, without letting it grow too long
why: Checklists are updated based on defect analysis: items lose effect as developers learn, and new high-severity defects add items, but the list must not grow too long.

distractorNotes.A: Checklists age; an unchanged list keeps checking errors that developers no longer make.
distractorNotes.B: Items also lose value as developers learn to avoid the same errors.
distractorNotes.C: New entries are for newly found high-severity defects, and the list must stay short.

stem: A studio uses a high-level checklist ("Check the audio", "Check the menus") for its regression testing. What is the most likely effect?
options: Less coverage and more repeatability
More variability between testers: potentially greater coverage but less repeatability
Full coverage of every requirement
The same results as fully scripted test cases
why: High-level checklists leave testers room to vary, which can increase coverage but makes the testing less repeatable.

distractorNotes.A: The reverse of the actual effect.
distractorNotes.C: Overgeneralisation: no checklist guarantees full coverage.
distractorNotes.D: Different testers will test differently, so results are not like scripted tests.

stem: Which statement about checklist-based testing is CORRECT?
options: It supports only functional testing
It can support various test types, including non-functional testing such as usability
It is only used in reviews, not in dynamic testing
It can only be used when detailed test cases exist
why: Checklists support functional and non-functional testing, e.g. a list of usability heuristics.

distractorNotes.A: Too narrow: non-functional testing is supported as well.
distractorNotes.C: Category smear with checklist-based reviewing (Chapter 3); checklist-based testing is dynamic.
distractorNotes.D: The reverse: checklists give guidance and some consistency when there are no detailed test cases.

stem: Before submitting a game to a console platform, the QA team works through the platform's requirements, phrased as questions such as "Does the game show the right message when the controller is disconnected?", and tests each one. Which technique is this?
options: Exploratory testing
Error guessing
Checklist-based testing
Acceptance test-driven development
why: Tests designed and executed to cover the test conditions on a list of questions: checklist-based testing.

distractorNotes.A: The test conditions are fixed in advance, not designed while learning.
distractorNotes.B: The list holds requirements to check, not anticipated defects.
distractorNotes.D: ATDD derives tests from a user story's acceptance criteria before implementation.

stem: Which are the three critical aspects of a user story?
options: Card, Collaboration, Completion
Concept, Conversation, Confirmation
Card, Conversation, Confirmation
Card, Code, Customer
why: Card (the medium), Conversation (how the software will be used), Confirmation (the acceptance criteria).

distractorNotes.A: Collaboration and Completion are not the aspects; it is Conversation and Confirmation.
distractorNotes.B: The first aspect is the Card, the medium that holds the story.
distractorNotes.D: Invented: code and customer are not aspects of a user story.

stem: In which of the three aspects of a user story are the acceptance criteria found?
options: Card
Conversation
Confirmation
Collaboration
why: The Confirmation is the acceptance criteria.

distractorNotes.A: The Card is the medium that holds the story.
distractorNotes.B: The criteria usually come out of the Conversation, but they are the Confirmation.
distractorNotes.D: Collaboration is not one of the three aspects.

stem: Which is the most common format for writing a user story?
options: Given [context], when [action], then [outcome]
As a [role], I want [goal to be accomplished], so that I can [resulting business value for the role]
As a developer, I will implement [component] by [date]
If [condition] then [action], else [other action]
why: The role–goal–value format, followed by the acceptance criteria.

distractorNotes.A: Given/When/Then is a scenario-oriented format for acceptance criteria.
distractorNotes.C: A task for a developer, not a feature valuable to a user.
distractorNotes.D: This is a decision rule, not a story.

stem: Story: "As a player, I want the whole online multiplayer mode, so that I can play with my friends." The team cannot estimate it or deliver it in one sprint. Which quality of a good user story does it most clearly lack?
options: Independent
Negotiable
Small
Testable
why: A story too large to estimate and deliver in a sprint lacks the quality of being small; it should be split.

distractorNotes.A: Nothing says it depends on other stories.
distractorNotes.B: Nothing says its details are fixed and cannot be discussed.
distractorNotes.D: Playing with friends can be checked; the problem is the size.

stem: Writing user stories collaboratively helps the team get a shared vision of what to deliver. Which three perspectives does this bring together?
options: Player, publisher and platform holder
Business, development and testing
Design, art and audio
Manager, author and reviewer
why: Collaborative authorship brings together the business, development and testing perspectives.

distractorNotes.A: These are stakeholders of a game, not the three perspectives named for user stories.
distractorNotes.C: Game disciplines, not the three perspectives.
distractorNotes.D: Category smear: these are review roles from Chapter 3.

stem: During refinement, the producer cannot say how she would check that a new story is done. What might this indicate?
options: The story is ready for implementation, because testing is the testers' job
The story may be unclear, may not reflect something valuable to her, or she may need help with testing
The story must be removed from the backlog
The acceptance criteria must be written after implementation
why: If a stakeholder does not know how to test a story, it may not be clear enough, may not be valuable to them, or they may just need help with testing.

distractorNotes.A: Wrong actor and a missed warning sign: stakeholders should understand how a story is confirmed.
distractorNotes.C: Overreaction: the story can be clarified rather than dropped.
distractorNotes.D: Acceptance criteria belong to the story before implementation; that is the point of the Confirmation.

stem: Which techniques can a team use to write user stories collaboratively?
options: Brainstorming and mind mapping
Inspections and walkthroughs
Fault attacks and error guessing
Statement and branch testing
why: Collaborative authorship of user stories can use brainstorming and mind mapping.

distractorNotes.B: Review types (Chapter 3) for examining work products, not for writing stories.
distractorNotes.C: Experience-based test techniques, not story-writing techniques.
distractorNotes.D: White-box test techniques.

stem: Which are the two most common formats for acceptance criteria?
options: Scenario-oriented and rule-oriented
Black-box and white-box
Formal and informal
Functional and non-functional
why: Scenario-oriented (e.g. Given/When/Then) and rule-oriented (e.g. a bullet-point verification list or an input–output table).

distractorNotes.B: These are families of test techniques.
distractorNotes.C: Not the format names in the syllabus.
distractorNotes.D: These are test types (WHAT vs HOW WELL), not formats.

stem: An acceptance criterion reads: "Given the player has 3 lives, when they fall off the map, then they respawn at the last checkpoint with 2 lives." Which format is this?
options: Rule-oriented
Scenario-oriented
State-oriented
Checklist-oriented
why: Given/When/Then describes a scenario: the scenario-oriented format used in BDD.

distractorNotes.A: Rule-oriented criteria are bullet-point verification lists or input–output tables.
distractorNotes.C: Not a syllabus format name.
distractorNotes.D: Not a syllabus format name; checklists belong to checklist-based testing.

stem: Acceptance criteria for a ranked reward are written as a table: Bronze rank → 100 coins; Silver → 250 coins; Gold → 500 coins; Platinum → 1000 coins. Which format is this?
options: Scenario-oriented
Given/When/Then
Behaviour-oriented
Rule-oriented
why: A table mapping inputs to outputs is a rule-oriented format.

distractorNotes.A: Scenario-oriented criteria describe scenarios, typically as Given/When/Then.
distractorNotes.B: Given/When/Then is the scenario-oriented example, not a table.
distractorNotes.C: Not a syllabus format name; behaviour is what BDD expresses in Given/When/Then.

stem: Which of the following is NOT a purpose of acceptance criteria?
options: Defining the scope of the user story
Describing how the developer will structure the code
Describing both positive and negative scenarios
Allowing accurate planning and estimation
why: Acceptance criteria say what must be true for the story to be accepted, not how it is implemented.

distractorNotes.A: Defining the scope is a purpose.
distractorNotes.C: Describing positive and negative scenarios is a purpose.
distractorNotes.D: Allowing accurate planning and estimation is a purpose.

stem: Which statement about acceptance criteria is CORRECT?
options: They describe only the positive scenarios of a story
They must always be written in Given/When/Then
From a testing view they are test conditions that tests should exercise
Testers write them alone, after the story is implemented
why: Acceptance criteria are the conditions the implementation must meet; for testing they are test conditions to be exercised, and the basis of acceptance testing.

distractorNotes.A: They describe positive and negative scenarios.
distractorNotes.B: Given/When/Then is one common format; rule-oriented and custom formats are allowed too.
distractorNotes.D: They usually come out of the Conversation, before implementation, with several perspectives.

stem: A team wants to write its acceptance criteria in its own house format rather than Given/When/Then or a rule list. Is that acceptable?
options: No: only the two standard formats are allowed
Yes, as long as the criteria are well-defined and unambiguous
Yes, but only for non-functional criteria
No: a custom format makes ATDD impossible
why: A custom format is fine if the acceptance criteria remain well-defined and unambiguous.

distractorNotes.A: The two are the most common formats, not the only allowed ones.
distractorNotes.C: There is no such restriction.
distractorNotes.D: ATDD works from the criteria, whatever their format, as long as they are clear.

stem: Story: "As a player, I want to rename my saved loadouts, so that I can find them quickly." Acceptance criteria: names are 1–20 characters; a name already in use is rejected with a message; renaming works offline. Following ATDD, which test case should be written FIRST?
options: Rename "Loadout 1" to "Sniper" and check that the new name appears in the list
Try a 21-character name and check that it is rejected
Measure that a rename completes within 200 ms
Rename a loadout to a name already in use and check the message
why: ATDD starts with positive test cases: the expected path with no errors or exceptions.

distractorNotes.B: A negative test case; it comes after the positive ones.
distractorNotes.C: Non-functional test cases come last (and this one is not in the criteria).
distractorNotes.D: A negative test case; it comes after the positive ones.

stem: Story: "As a guild leader, I want to remove inactive members, so that the guild stays active." AC1: only the leader can remove members. AC2: a removed member gets a notification. AC3: a member inactive for less than 14 days cannot be removed. AC4: every removal is recorded in the guild log. Tests: T1 the leader removes a member inactive for 20 days, who gets a notification; T2 an officer tries to remove a member and is refused; T3 the leader tries to remove a member inactive for 10 days and is refused. Which acceptance criterion has no test case yet?
options: AC1
AC2
AC3
AC4
why: T1 covers AC2 (and the positive side of AC1 and AC3), T2 covers AC1, T3 covers AC3. Nothing checks the guild log: AC4.

distractorNotes.A: T2 checks that a non-leader is refused, and T1 that the leader can remove.
distractorNotes.B: T1 checks the notification.
distractorNotes.C: T3 checks the 14-day rule (and T1 the other side of it).

stem: Story: "As a player, I want to mute individual players in voice chat, so that I don't hear them." Acceptance criteria: a player can be muted from the scoreboard; a muted player stays muted for the rest of the match; muting affects only the player who mutes.
